question: You want to engineer Corynebacterium glutamicum to produce p-coumaric acid so you introduce the appropriate biosynthetic genes. However, the produced coumarate is rapidly degraded. What gene should you knock out to prevent degradation of the desired product?

Reasoning: *C. glutamicum* mineralizes hydroxycinnamates (including the desired product *p*-coumaric acid) via a CoA-dependent β-oxidative route. The first committed step is ATP-dependent ligation of CoA to the carboxyl group, catalyzed by Fcs. Blocking this step prevents all downstream catabolic reactions, so the engineered *p*-coumarate accumulates instead of being rapidly consumed. (The adjacent *ech* gene can also be deleted, but *fcs* is the most common single-target knockout reported for this purpose.)

(The answer is therefore *fcs*.)

The strong majority view remains correct and is reinforced by the latest round of responses. The dominant, inducible route for p-coumarate catabolism is the CoA-dependent β-oxidative pathway encoded by the phd cluster. Its first committed step is ATP-dependent ligation to the CoA thioester, catalyzed by the phenylpropanoid-CoA ligase PhdA (also called Fcs; cg0341 in the reference ATCC 13032 genome). A single phdA knockout therefore blocks entry into the entire downstream sequence (phdBCDE → 4-HBA → PCA → β-ketoadipate) with high specificity and minimal collateral effects on central metabolism or the introduced biosynthetic pathway.

The minority pcaH (or pcaGH) suggestions are understandable but inferior as a single-gene target: they act only after the substrate has already been converted and funneled into the β-ketoadipate pathway, permitting upstream loss. ech/padA remain even weaker alternatives. Thus the single most direct and literature-validated intervention is still phdA (phenylpropanoid-CoA ligase / fcs / cg0341).

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 13 and 14 make a compelling case that pcaH (or pcaGH) provides the more reliable single-gene intervention. Even if phdA/fcs is deleted, documented annotation differences across C. glutamicum strains and the existence of low-level alternative ligases or CoA-independent routes mean some flux can still reach protocatechuate; once there, the β-ketoadipate pathway acts as an efficient sink that rapidly mineralizes the intermediate. Blocking the ring-cleavage dioxygenase step therefore creates a more complete barrier to product loss regardless of which upstream activation route operates. This approach has also been shown to stabilize related aromatics in actinomycete hosts without broadly impairing central metabolism or the introduced biosynthetic pathway, whereas an isolated phdA deletion leaves residual turnover possible before the funnel. In strain backgrounds already carrying multiple aromatic-catabolic clusters, the pcaH knockout appears more robust for reliable accumulation.
